title: Spine MRI: Degeneration, Compression and Trauma
goal: Report displaced lumbar disc material in the agreed nomenclature, and separate the spinal emergencies from the incidental findings.

quiz.prompt: On the sagittal T2 image at L5/S1 the displaced disc material behind the vertebral body measures 13 mm craniocaudally at its widest, while its neck where it leaves the disc space measures 7 mm in the same plane. It occupies about 15 per cent of the disc circumference and remains continuous with the parent disc. How should this be reported in the standard lumbar disc nomenclature?
choices: A disc extrusion
A disc protrusion
A broad-based bulge
A sequestered fragment
quiz.explain: The rule is geometric, and it is the only thing separating the first two words. Measure the greatest distance between the edges of the displaced material, then the distance between the edges of its base in the same plane: if the material beyond the disc space is wider than its base - 13 mm against a 7 mm neck - it is an extrusion, and if it is narrower or equal it is a protrusion. Continuity with the parent disc keeps it out of the sequestration category, which is reserved for a fragment that has lost that continuity. A bulge is a different animal altogether: disc tissue extending beyond the ring apophyses around more than a quarter of the circumference, a contour rather than a herniation, and 15 per cent is too little in any case. The words are not interchangeable in a report, because extrusions are more often symptomatic, more likely to migrate, and - counter-intuitively - more likely to resorb spontaneously, since exposed nucleus pulposus provokes a vascularised inflammatory response. Measure in the plane where the ratio is greatest: a herniation that looks contained on the sagittal may be an extrusion on the axial, and one plane is enough to make it one.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old with severe right L5 radiculopathy has an ovoid mass in the right lateral recess at the level of the L4 vertebral body, separate from the L4/5 disc, slightly brighter than that disc on T2, with a thin rim of enhancement after gadolinium and no central enhancement. What is it most likely to be?
choices: A migrated sequestered disc fragment
A synovial cyst from the facet joint
A nerve sheath tumour on the root
An early epidural abscess collection
quiz.explain: Three features do the work. A fragment lying separate from its parent disc, having travelled cranially or caudally in the epidural space, is a sequestration; it is often brighter than the degenerate parent disc on T2 because it is hydrated and inflamed; and it typically shows a thin peripheral rim of enhancement from surrounding granulation tissue with a non-enhancing avascular centre. A nerve sheath tumour enhances solidly and throughout, is centred on the root rather than in the recess, and over time widens the foramen or scallops bone. A synovial cyst arises from a degenerate facet joint, sits posterolaterally against it, and usually has a low-signal rim and a demonstrable connection to the joint. An abscess would come with disc and endplate destruction, marrow oedema and systemic signs. The reporting consequence is practical: a fragment resorbs in a substantial proportion of patients, and if it is to be removed the surgeon needs to be told the parent level and the direction and distance of migration, because a fragment behind a vertebral body is not reached through a standard interlaminar approach to the disc.

quiz.prompt: A patient with recurrent left leg pain nine months after L5/S1 microdiscectomy has soft tissue in the left anterior epidural space at the operated level. Explain how you would use contrast to decide whether this is fibrosis or recurrent disc material, and why the timing of the post-contrast images matters.
quiz.answer: Give gadolinium and image early, within roughly ten to fifteen minutes. Epidural fibrosis is vascularised granulation tissue: it enhances immediately, homogeneously and throughout its substance, and it tends to be retractile rather than mass-like, drawing the thecal sac and root towards it. Recurrent disc material is avascular and does not enhance itself; what enhances is the vascularised tissue around it, so on early images it shows a peripheral rim of enhancement with a non-enhancing centre, and it is polypoid, has mass effect, and is continuous with the disc space. The timing matters because contrast diffuses passively into disc material over time, so on images acquired thirty minutes or more after injection the recurrent disc fills in and becomes indistinguishable from scar, turning a reliable sign into a misleading one.
quiz.explain: The distinction changes management directly, which is why it is worth protocolling properly: recurrent disc material can be re-operated, whereas re-operating on scar tends to make the patient worse and is the classic route into failed back surgery syndrome. Two refinements keep the sign honest. The two often coexist, so the question in practice is which component accounts for the mass effect on the symptomatic root, not which one is present. And mass effect is itself part of the argument - scar retracts and follows the contours of the thecal sac, disc material pushes. If the study cannot be done early after injection, say so in the report rather than calling the appearance for one or the other.

quiz.prompt: CT and MRI of the thoracolumbar junction show a burst fracture of L1 with retropulsion, the patient is neurologically intact, and STIR shows a widened interspinous space with high signal through the interspinous and supraspinous ligaments. What is the TLICS total? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: TLICS adds three components. Morphology: compression 1, burst 2, translation or rotation 3, distraction 4 - here 2. Neurological status: intact 0, nerve root 2, complete cord or conus injury 2, incomplete cord or conus injury 3, cauda equina 3 - here 0. Posterior ligamentous complex: intact 0, indeterminate 2, disrupted 3 - here 3, because interspinous widening with frank ligamentous high signal is disruption rather than suspicion. Total 5. A score of 3 or less is managed non-operatively, 4 is equivocal, and 5 or more points to surgery, so the MRI has just moved a neurologically intact patient into the operative group. That is the reason MRI is added to CT when the CT shows a burst fracture and the posterior elements are in doubt, and it is why the system weights the posterior ligamentous complex so heavily: it is the structure that governs mechanical stability and the one CT judges least well.

quiz.prompt: Put these four descriptions of displaced lumbar disc material in order of increasing displacement from the disc space, as the standard nomenclature grades them.
quiz.explain: A bulge is not a herniation at all: it is disc tissue extending beyond the ring apophyses around more than a quarter of the circumference, a generalised change of contour that usually reflects age and degeneration. A protrusion is a localised herniation whose base is at least as wide as any part of the material beyond the disc space. An extrusion is a localised herniation that is wider beyond the disc space than at its base, so its neck is narrower than its dome. A sequestration is an extrusion that has lost continuity with the parent disc altogether. One term is often confused with this last: migration describes displacement away from the site of extrusion, cranially or caudally, and a migrated fragment may or may not be sequestered - the two words answer different questions, one about position and one about continuity.

quiz.prompt: A woman with metastatic breast cancer is referred for lumbar MRI because of two weeks of back pain. The lumbar study shows an epidural soft-tissue mass at T12 indenting the conus, and she has brisk reflexes in the legs and a sensory level. What is the most important next imaging step?
choices: MRI of the whole spine before treatment is planned
CT of the same level to assess the bony detail
Bone scintigraphy to stage the rest of the skeleton
Repeat MRI after dexamethasone has been started
quiz.answer: MRI of the whole spine before treatment is planned
quiz.explain: Roughly a third of patients with metastatic epidural spinal cord compression have compressive disease at more than one level, and the second site is often clinically silent because the first one is producing all the symptoms. Radiotherapy fields and surgical plans are drawn from the full extent of disease, so imaging only the symptomatic level risks treating one deposit and leaving another to compress the cord a fortnight later; national guidance accordingly asks for urgent whole-spine MRI in anyone with suspected metastatic cord compression. The distractors each answer a real but secondary question: CT characterises bone and vertebral body integrity for surgical planning, scintigraphy stages the skeleton, and steroids are started immediately - but none of them changes the immediate decision the way the extent of compressive disease does, and starting steroids is never a reason to delay or repeat the MRI.

quiz.prompt: Two patients each have a large central disc extrusion: one at T9/T10 and one at L4/L5. Explain what determines whether the picture is cord compression or cauda equina compression, what each looks like clinically, and how far the MRI must extend.
quiz.answer: The determinant is the level of the conus medullaris, which in adults ends at about T12 to L1, with the lower limit of normal around the L2/L3 disc; a compressive lesion above it presses on the cord, one below it presses on the cauda equina. The T9/T10 extrusion therefore causes cord compression, with upper motor neurone signs below the level: spasticity, brisk reflexes, extensor plantars, a sensory level, and T2 signal change within the cord if compression has been sustained. The L4/L5 extrusion compresses nerve roots and gives lower motor neurone signs: flaccid weakness, absent reflexes, bilateral radicular pain, saddle anaesthesia, and urinary retention with overflow incontinence. The MRI must cover the whole lumbosacral spine down to the sacrum, because a compressive lesion below the volume scanned is simply missed, and it must extend upwards whenever the signs are of cord rather than root disease, since the true upper level of the lesion may lie well above the symptomatic dermatome.
quiz.explain: Getting the compartment right is what makes the request sensible, because a referral for 'cord compression' at L4/5 asks for something anatomically impossible and often produces a scan that stops too high. Two refinements matter at the bedside. A conus lesion mixes the two pictures - early and severe bladder involvement with a combination of upper and lower motor neurone signs - and is the reason the transition zone is described separately. And retention is a late feature of cauda equina compression rather than an early one, so waiting for it before requesting the scan is how the diagnosis gets made too late; a raised post-void residual and loss of perianal sensation are the findings that should trigger imaging out of hours.

quiz.prompt: An 80-year-old with back pain after lifting has a collapsed L2 vertebral body. MRI shows a band of low T1 and high STIR signal running parallel to and beneath the superior endplate, with normal fatty marrow preserved through the rest of the body, retropulsion of the posterosuperior corner, normal pedicles and no paravertebral soft tissue. What does this favour?
choices: An acute osteoporotic insufficiency fracture
Metastatic collapse from an occult primary
Vertebral osteomyelitis with early collapse
Myelomatous involvement of the body
quiz.explain: Five features in the stem point the same way. Band-like oedema parallel to the fractured endplate with normal marrow preserved elsewhere in the body means the marrow has been bruised, not replaced, whereas tumour replaces marrow diffusely and completely. Retropulsion of the posterosuperior corner is a mechanical failure pattern, while a convex bulge of the posterior cortex suggests an expanding tumour. Sparing of the pedicles matters because metastatic disease reaches the vertebra through the vascular supply of the posterior body and commonly takes the pedicle with it. And the absence of paravertebral or epidural soft tissue is decisive: tumour and infection both make soft tissue, mechanical failure does not. A fluid sign - a linear T2-bright cleft within the body - is another benign feature. Infection separates itself on the disc, which it destroys along with both adjacent endplates, whereas a fracture leaves the disc alone. Where the picture is genuinely equivocal, follow-up at six to twelve weeks showing resolving oedema, or a biopsy, settles it; diffusion helps but overlaps.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old with chronic mechanical back pain has low T1 and high T2 signal in the marrow on both sides of the L4/5 disc. The disc space is narrowed, the disc itself is dark on T2 with a preserved intranuclear cleft, the endplates are irregular but continuous, and there is no paraspinal or epidural soft tissue. Inflammatory markers are normal. What does this represent?
choices: Type 1 degenerative endplate marrow change
Pyogenic discitis with early osteomyelitis
Metastasis crossing the L4/5 disc space
An acute Schmorl node with marrow oedema
quiz.explain: The marrow signal is identical in the two leading diagnoses - that is the trap, and it is why the disc rather than the marrow decides the case. In degenerative type 1 change the disc is desiccated and dark on T2 and keeps its intranuclear cleft, the endplates are irregular from wear but their cortical line is continuous, and there is no soft tissue. In pyogenic infection the disc is bright on T2 and loses the cleft early, the endplates are eroded with loss of the cortical line, and there is paraspinal or epidural inflammatory tissue that enhances. Type 1 change is vascularised fibrous marrow with oedema, and its natural history is to convert to type 2, fatty (bright on T1, iso to bright on T2), and later to type 3, sclerotic (dark on both). It matters because type 1 is the type most associated with pain and the one most often mistaken for infection. The exception that keeps a reader honest is tuberculous spondylitis, which tends to spare the disc and spread beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament, so a preserved disc does not exclude infection when the clinical picture fits.

quiz.prompt: A restrained front-seat passenger in a frontal collision has a fracture line running horizontally through the spinous process, both pedicles and the posterior body of L2, with anterior wedging, and bruising across the lower abdomen. Beyond the spine, what does this pattern oblige you to look for on the same CT?
choices: Bowel and mesenteric injury in the abdomen
Renal pedicle avulsion at the vascular hilum
Diaphragmatic rupture on the left side
Aortic injury at the level of the isthmus
quiz.answer: Bowel and mesenteric injury in the abdomen
quiz.explain: This is a flexion-distraction, or Chance, injury: the lap belt acts as a fulcrum across the abdomen, the spine hinges over it, the posterior elements fail in tension and the anterior body fails in compression. The same mechanism crushes bowel and mesentery between belt and spine, and the association is strong enough that the fracture should be treated as a marker for visceral injury - small bowel perforation, mesenteric tear and delayed devascularisation being the injuries that get missed on the first pass. Look for free fluid without solid organ injury, mesenteric fat stranding, bowel wall thickening and extraluminal gas. The spinal half of the answer is that this is a distraction morphology with a disrupted posterior ligamentous complex, which places it in the operative range even in a neurologically intact patient. It is also easy to miss on axial images alone, because a horizontal fracture line can run between slices: the sagittal reformats are where it is seen.

quiz.prompt: On a lateral radiograph of the thoracic spine a wedged vertebral body measures 13 mm in anterior height and 24 mm in posterior height, and the vertebrae above and below are of normal shape. Taking the posterior height as the reference, what percentage of the anterior height has been lost? Give the answer to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: The loss is (24 - 13) / 24, which is 11/24, or 45.8 per cent, so 46 per cent. The semiquantitative Genant grading reads those bands as roughly 20 to 25 per cent height loss for grade 1 (mild), 25 to 40 per cent for grade 2 (moderate), and more than 40 per cent for grade 3 (severe), applied to anterior height (wedge), middle height (biconcave) or posterior height (crush). This vertebra is a grade 3 wedge deformity. Two practical points travel with the arithmetic. The reference should be the posterior height of the same vertebra when the neighbours are themselves deformed, since comparing with an abnormal neighbour understates the loss. And a vertebral fracture found on any imaging, including one seen incidentally on a CT requested for something else, is an osteoporotic fracture until proved otherwise and is among the strongest predictors of the next one, so it belongs in the conclusion of the report rather than buried in a list of degenerative findings.

quiz.prompt: A CT shows an L1 burst fracture in a neurologically intact patient, and the surgical team asks whether the posterior ligamentous complex is intact. State the sequence you would rely on, the findings that indicate disruption, and why the determination changes the plan.
quiz.answer: Sagittal STIR, or another fat-suppressed T2-weighted sequence; fat suppression is what makes ligamentous and interspinous oedema visible against fatty marrow and epidural fat. Disruption is indicated by high signal within or frank discontinuity of the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments and the ligamentum flavum, widening of the interspinous distance compared with the levels above and below, fluid or widening in the facet joints, a perched or dislocated facet, and avulsion at a ligamentous attachment. It changes the plan because the posterior ligamentous complex is the principal restraint against progressive kyphosis and translation: with it intact, a burst fracture in a neurologically intact patient is usually braced, and with it disrupted the same fracture scores into the operative range and is stabilised. CT can only infer the state of the ligaments from bony spacing, which is why MRI is added whenever the answer would change management.
quiz.explain: The reason the classification systems put so much weight here is that the posterior ligamentous complex heals poorly, so a disrupted complex means the deformity will progress even if the bone unites. Two cautions keep the report defensible. MRI over-calls: isolated high signal in the interspinous fat or in the ligamentum flavum alone is common after any injury and is not by itself disruption, which is why the classification offers an 'indeterminate' category worth two points rather than forcing a binary. And the findings should be read together - widened interspinous distance with fluid in the facet joints and discontinuous ligaments is a different report from one equivocal finding in isolation. Say which of the three states you believe the complex is in, because the score, and the operation, follow from that word.

approach.step: Decide bulge or herniation on circumference
approach.detail: Displacement around the whole circumference is a bulge and is not a herniation. Focal displacement of less than 25% of the circumference is a herniation.

approach.step: Then protrusion or extrusion, on geometry alone
approach.detail: Compare the widest part of the displaced material with its base. Narrower than the base is a protrusion; wider is an extrusion.
Migration is displacement away from the site of extrusion. Sequestration is loss of continuity with the parent disc — and it changes the surgical plan.
Central, subarticular (lateral recess), foraminal, extraforaminal. Say which, because it predicts the root.
Disc level, suprapedicular, pedicular, infrapedicular — the level a migrated fragment has reached.
Modic change, and vertical herniation through an endplate gap — a Schmorl node.

classify.note: Axial zones: central, subarticular (lateral recess), foraminal, extraforaminal. Craniocaudal levels: disc, suprapedicular, pedicular, infrapedicular.

measure.how: Judge the arc of displaced disc on the axial image.
measure.cutoff: 50–100% of the circumference is a bulge · 25–50% is a broad-based herniation · < 25% is focal

measure.how: Distinguish from a broad-based herniation before you report it.
measure.cutoff: > 25% of circumference — adaptation to adjacent deformity

measure.how: Edge-to-edge width of the displaced material against edge-to-edge width of its base, in whichever plane is widest.
Uncommon, and symptoms are severe because the dorsal root ganglion sits in the foramen.

modifiers.meaning: Low T1, high T2 — fibrovascular tissue, inflammatory change, perhaps oedema. Correlates with low back pain.
High T1, isointense or high T2 — bone marrow replaced by fat.
Low T1, low T2 — reactive sclerosis.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
MRI lumbar spine: sagittal T1 and T2, axial T2 through [levels].

FINDINGS
Alignment and vertebral height: [ ].
Marrow: [normal / Modic 1, 2 or 3 at — ].
Per level [L1-2 to L5-S1]:
  Disc: [normal / degenerate / bulge / protrusion / extrusion], [contained / uncontained], [migrated — level / sequestrated].
  Zone: [central / subarticular / foraminal / extraforaminal], [left / right].
  Annular fissure: [absent / present].
  Canal: [ ]. Lateral recess: [ ]. Foramen: [ ].
  Root contacted, displaced or compressed: [ ].
Conus at [level]. Cord and cauda equina signal: [normal / abnormal].

IMPRESSION
1. [Level, term, zone, side, and the root affected.]
2. [Sequestrated fragment and where it has migrated to, if present.]
3. [Any finding that is an emergency rather than degeneration.]
pitfalls: Calling a circumferential bulge a herniation. A bulge involves the whole circumference; a herniation is focal and under 25%.
Using 'protrusion' and 'extrusion' loosely. The distinction is purely geometric — displaced material narrower than its base, or wider.
Not saying whether a fragment is sequestrated. Loss of continuity with the parent disc is what the surgeon needs, and it is a separate statement from migration.
Skipping the zone. The subarticular recess is the commonest site because the posterior longitudinal ligament is thin there, and the zone predicts which root is caught.
Under-calling a foraminal herniation because it is small. Only 5–10% are foraminal or further out, and symptoms are severe because the dorsal root ganglion sits there.
